system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-05-09 21:32:00 to 2145-05-14 14:54:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with flank pain, fever, and dark, cloudy urine, consistent with recurrent pyelonephritis due to a left ureteroileal conduit anastomotic stricture. He was treated with a two-week course of IV daptomycin and tobramycin, dosed safely per his chronic kidney disease. A PICC line was placed for antibiotic administration. His infection resolved, pain improved, and kidney function remained stable. Amlodipine was discontinued due to normotension, and Renagel was replaced with sevelamer. He was discharged home with follow-up appointments in urology and primary care, and instructions to monitor for recurrence of infection.
problems: Other artificial opening of urinary tract status
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  BILATERAL FEET RADIOGRAPHS

INDICATION:  ___ male with foot ulcers on pain. Evaluate for
osteomyelitis.

TECHNIQUE:  Two views of each foot were obtained.

COMPARISON:  None available.

FINDINGS: 

RIGHT FOOT: There is severe osteopenia of the right foot which could mask
nondisplaced and stress fractures. Allowing for this limitation, there is no
fracture or dislocation. Severe degenerative changes are demonstrated, with
deformities of the toes. There is edema at the dorsum of the foot overlying
the metatarsum but there is no clear bony destructive lesion to suggest
osteomyelitis.

LEFT FOOT: There is severe osteopenia which could mask nondisplaced and stress
fractures. Allowing for this limitation, there is no fracture or acute
dislocation.  Lateral subluxation of the IP joint of the ___ toe is likely
degenerative. There is soft tissue swelling but no clear lysis of the bone. 
Severe degenerative changes are demonstrated, with deformities of the toes.
There is edema at the dorsum of the foot overlying the metatarsum but there is
no clear bony destructive lesion to suggest osteomyelitis.

IMPRESSION: 

Severe osteopenia bilaterally. No fracture identified. No obvious lesion
concerning for osteomyelitis allowing for limitations of this exam. If
clinical concern remains an MR should be considered.

INDICATION:  ___ male paraplegic h/o neurogenic bladder s/pileal conduit w/
longstanding history of bouts of pyelonephritis, left anastamotic
ureteral-conduitstricture treated with PCNU. Patient presents for routine
exchange.  // Routine PCNU stent exchange please also a evaluate distal ureter
for possible operative reaanastomosis to loop

COMPARISON:  Prior stent exchange images from ___ and loopogram from ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology resident
and Dr. ___, attending radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
___ supervised and participated in the entire procedure.

ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
200 mcg of fentanyl and 4mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 45 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site

MEDICATIONS: Topical viscous lidocaine and injected 1% subcutaneous lidocaine,
1 g IV meropenem, a Versed and fentanyl as described above.

CONTRAST: 25ml of Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  ___, 48mGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Over the wire ureterogram/nephrostogram. and exchange of indwelling
percutaneous neck for ureteral stent for new 8 ___ by 22 cm stent.
PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient by ___
___, ___. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and
placed prone on the exam table.  1 g of Meropenum was administered
intravenously. A pre-procedure time-out using a checklist was performed per
___ protocol.

A scout image was obtained over the abdomen. Skin and subcutaneous shin
tissues of the exit site of the catheter were infiltrated with 1% lidocaine
and the hub of the catheter was cut off to release the upper pigtail
formation. A 0.035 ___ wire was advanced through the catheter under
fluoroscopic visualization, however this could not traverse the distal 2 cm of
the stent where it appear to be occluded. Exchange is made for 0.035 stiff
angled glidewire which was able to traverse the distal stent and with wire
extending through the patient's ostomy bag, the nephro ureteral stent was
removed over the wire and replaced with a 5 ___ long Kumpe catheter which
was advanced to the level of the distal ileal loop to allow placement of a
0.035 ___ wire. Over the ___ wire, a 25 cm long 7 ___ sheath was
advanced to the level of the distal ureter and a pull-back ureterogram was
performed over this, but because this sheath did not reach beyond the
patient's ureteral stenosis, exchange is made for a longer, 35 cm 6 ___
sheath over which pull-back ureterogram was recorded digitally. Based on this,
telephone call was made to Dr. ___ and after discussion of and
review of the findings, the sheath was removed to allow passage of a new 8
___ shorter ureteral stent. A 22 cm stent was placed because patient was
bothered by the distal loop extending beyond his stoma.  The loop was formed
and locked and the digital image was recorded.  Contrast was injected to
assure stent patency and this was then flushed with saline.  The drain was
capped. Findings were discussed with the patient. This was sutured to the skin
with a single silk suture and also secured with a Stat Lock device as had been
present previously.  A dry sterile dressing was placed and the patient was
transferred back to the Radiology care unit.

FINDINGS: 

The patient's indwelling 8 ___ by 22 cm nephro ureteral stent was in
functional position with the upper pigtail at the level of the low lower left
renal pelvis. Upon removal, the distal portion of the stent had adherent
tissue with an appearance of ileal mucosa. This occluded the distal portion of
the pigtail but some side holes from the loop or patent.

The left renal collecting system is dilated and the upper ureter is tortuous,
unchanged from for prior studies. Pull-back ureterogram demonstrated most
significant area of left ureteral stenosis at the level of the mid sacrum,
approximately 6 cm proximal to the expected level of the anastomosis with the
loop. Injection of contrast just proximal to than stenosis flows retrograde up
into the upper collecting system only. Diffusely thin ureter distal to this
appears to be a collapsed normal ureter. The contrast filled ileal loop has a
normal appearance. Final image shows both pigtails of the 8 ___ by 22 cm
stent in good position with contrast flow from the upper left collecting
system down to the loop. This distal pigtail is just beyond the anastomosis
and should not be able to pass forward through the patient's stoma.

Note is also made of the lower ends of intact metallic spinal rods.

IMPRESSION: 

Persistent dilatation of left upper collecting system above left ureteral
stenosis at the level of the sacrum, several cm proximal to the anastomosis
with the ileal loop. Images reviewed with and discussed with Dr. ___
___ via telephone. Replacement of new slightly shorter 8 ___ by 22 cm
nephro ureteral stent which is capped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital now after coming in through the ER. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I started feeling weird yesterday afternoon—dizzy and kind of out of it. I went to the bathroom and pulled down my socks, and my left foot was raw and red. Right foot’s got some sores too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And since you have paraplegia, you can’t feel pain in your feet, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I didn’t feel a thing. But I saw the redness and called 911. I also had chills and sweats, though I didn’t think I had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’re concerned about cellulitis—an infection in the skin and soft tissue—especially on your left foot. We also noticed some new pressure ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pressure ulcers? But I had socks on. Why didn’t anyone check my feet last time I was here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your frustration. From your records, it looks like you declined a foot exam during your last admission. But we’re going to be more thorough this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want things missed again. I’ve had MRSA before, and I don’t need another bad infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking that seriously. You were given vancomycin in the ER, but you had a reaction—itching and welts. Is vancomycin on your allergy list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I think so. I’ve had bad reactions before. Was it bad this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was a rash and throat itchiness, but we treated it quickly with Benadryl and steroids. You’re stable now. Because of the allergy, we’re switching to a different antibiotic—linezolid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, linezolid is safe for your kidney function. We’re monitoring your labs closely. Your creatinine is a bit higher than usual—3.6—but we expect that with infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s been bothering me near the nephrostomy tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that. Your urine showed some white cells, but the initial culture was contaminated. We’ll repeat it. Right now, we don’t think it’s a kidney infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I just had one of those a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. We’re also scheduling a nephrostomy tube exchange—it’s routine for you, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, every few months. It helps keep the urine draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll do that early in the week. For now, we’ve started wound care on your feet. The team recommends special boots—waffle boots—to protect them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do whatever it takes. I don’t want to lose a toe or worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. White count was high at 13.3 yesterday, now it’s coming down. That means the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any word on the foot X-rays?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fractures. Severe osteopenia, which makes it hard to rule out bone infection completely, but no clear signs of osteomyelitis. We don’t think the bone is involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just skin and soft tissue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re confident it’s cellulitis and pressure ulcers. The wound care team will change your dressings daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new antibiotic—linezolid—is it working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect it to. You’ll need to finish a full 10-day course, including after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that. What about my other meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your usual meds: levetiracetam for seizures, sevelamer for phosphate control, sodium bicarbonate, and your pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Percocet, but it’s not helping like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched you to oxycodone SR—OxyContin—60mg every 8 hours. It’s stronger and longer-acting. We also added tizanidine for muscle spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my sleep meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered your trazodone from 50mg to 25mg. Linezolid can interact with higher doses. You can go back up after you finish the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve been anxious. Can I still take my alprazolam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. We know this has been stressful. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your urine culture grew E. coli, but it’s sensitive to the linezolid and other antibiotics. No need to change treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same bug from my last infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You have a history of recurrent UTIs with E. coli, Pseudomonas, and Enterococcus. But this time, it’s likely from the skin, not your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No growth. That’s reassuring—means the infection hasn’t spread to your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is now 7.9—completely normal. The cellulitis is improving. Redness is less, and no new ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still some discomfort, but it’s stable. We think it’s from the nephrostomy site, not a new infection. We’ll address it during tomorrow’s tube exchange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nephrostomy tube was successfully replaced today. The radiologist said the stent is in good position and draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they see anything unusual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The old stent had some tissue blocking the end, but the new one is clear. There’s still a stricture in the ureter, but the stent is bypassing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The urologist will discuss options later. For now, the stent is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Continue linezolid for 10 days total, wound care with the boots, and follow up with urology and nephrology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mom is my power of attorney—she’ll help me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve spoken with her. She’ll get your discharge instructions and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is over. I just want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can to prevent that. Keep your skin clean, check your feet daily with help, and call if you see redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening—even when I was upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have every right to be heard. We’re here to care for you, not just treat the illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your meds and wound care. You’ll be ready to go in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with cellulitis and new pressure ulcers on both feet, discovered after he noticed redness and raw skin while being unable to feel pain due to paraplegia. He had a prior allergic reaction to vancomycin in the ED, prompting a switch to linezolid, which led to clinical improvement. Wound care was initiated, and a scheduled nephrostomy tube exchange was performed without complications. His infection resolved, white blood cell count normalized, and back pain stabilized. He was discharged home with instructions to complete a 10-day course of linezolid, continue protective foot care with waffle boots, and follow up with urology, nephrology, and plastic surgery.
